activities.anchor: Drawings are the instructions, and reading them is a tested skill
activities.caption: pair each drawing element with what it tells you
activities.name: amtDrawingMatch

config.prompt: Drawings are the legal instructions — pair each element with its meaning:

pairs.right: several flat views (front, top, side) of one object, each aligned with the others
the allowed wiggle room around a measurement
electrical logic — symbols and wire numbers, not physical routing
using a superseded one is using wrong data — a regulatory event, not just a mistake

config.why: Schematics are the system cousins: the mechanic's diagnostic work usually begins by tracing a schematic to form a hypothesis before touching hardware.

activities.anchor: is mostly applied arithmetic with careful units
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the fuel load's weight
activities.name: amtFuelEstimate

config.prompt: Avgas weighs about 0.72 kg per litre. Roughly what does 120 litres of fuel weigh?
config.why: 120 × 0.72 ≈ 86 kg — and converting between the systems (2.54 cm per inch, 2.2 lb per kg) is why units are carried through every step: a 90-kg fuel load becoming 90 litres is only survivable as one of them.
config.context: Precision matters at the tool level too: micrometers and calipers read to thousandths, and tolerances are computed, not guessed.

activities.anchor: The FAA General Handbook opens with physics because the hangar uses it daily
activities.caption: which curve is the torque trade-off?
activities.name: amtLeverTrace

config.prompt: Torque = force × length. Which curve shows the hand force needed for a 35 N·m bolt as wrench length (x) grows?

curves.label: A: inverse — longer lever, less force

config.why: F = 35/x — double the length, halve the force. The torque wrench is a calibrated lever, which is exactly why extra length silently destroys its reading.

activities.anchor: The regulatory layer is what makes an AMT different from a good mechanic
activities.caption: file the rule — which regulation owns it?
activities.name: amtRegBuckets

config.prompt: Two parts and one paper trail — file each fact:

items.label: defines the mechanic certificate — Airframe and/or Powerplant ratings
defines what maintenance legally means — inspection, overhaul, repair, preservation
the performance rules: methods acceptable to the Administrator, calibrated instruments
Form 337 documents major repairs and alterations
an uncomplied airworthiness directive grounds the aircraft

config.why: The certificate defines privileges and limits; Part 43 defines the work; the logbooks carry every entry with date, description, reference data and signature — the paper trail is the safety system.

activities.anchor: The paperwork system has named artefacts
activities.caption: rebuild the paper trail, from finding to signing
activities.name: amtPaperOrder

config.prompt: The document chain that makes work legally exist — put it in order:
items: the FAA finds a safety problem and issues an airworthiness directive
the AD becomes legally mandatory — an uncomplied one grounds the aircraft
the technician performs the correction per approved data and tools
the logbook entry records date, description, reference data and signature
inspection by someone other than the performer closes the loop
config.why: Verification by someone other than the performer, against published standards, recorded permanently — that is the whole system in one sentence, and falsifying it is a federal offence.

activities.anchor: The General curriculum's habits show in the tool box
activities.caption: drag the divider — tool box versus tool control
activities.name: amtToolCompare

config.prompt: Two tool cultures — drag between them:

before.label: Ordinary tool box
before.text: Tools live where they land; a forgotten wrench is tomorrow's tidy-up.

after.label: Shadowed tool control
after.text: Every tool has an outlined home and inventories are checked at shift end — because a forgotten wrench in an engine bay is a foreign-object-damage event waiting for the next flight.

config.why: A tool's accuracy is a document, not an assumption: the calibration chain from wrench to national standard is what makes 'torque to 35 N·m' mean the same thing in every hangar on Earth.

activities.anchor: a bolt that feels tight is tight enough
activities.caption: true or false — the wrist versus the wrench
activities.name: amtBoltJudge

statements.s: The clamp a bolt produces comes from controlled stretch inside its torque range.
statements.why: Stress and strain are the daily physics: the bolt is a calibrated spring, not a screw of infinite strength.

statements.s: A bolt that feels tight is tight enough.
statements.why: The trade measures torque instead of trusting the wrist — a few degrees of turn separate clamped-for-life from fatigued-and-waiting-to-fail.

statements.s: Torque wrenches are stored unwound to protect the spring.
statements.why: Used smoothly to a stop, stored unwound, and calibrated on schedule with traceable certificates.

statements.s: An untraceable torque value is still a known torque value.
statements.why: An untraceable torque value is an unknown torque value — the document chain is what makes the number mean anything.

activities.anchor: The weight-and-balance arithmetic deserves its worked example
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the CG arithmetic
activities.name: amtCgSpot

config.prompt: This weight-and-balance summary contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Total moment ≈ 1,787 kg·m over 836 kg gives a CG near 2.14 m aft of datum.
The certified window (2.00–2.30 m) is the verdict.
Burning fuel leaves the CG where it started, so one check at takeoff covers the whole flight.
A heavy pilot plus full fuel can pass the weight limit while failing the CG limit.
config.correction: Burning fuel MOVES the CG — the tank's arm no longer carries its moment — so the check is done for takeoff AND landing weights.
config.why: Two separate gates, both mandatory: total moment over total weight gives the CG, and fuel burn reshuffles the moments in flight.
